title: The Small Letters
premise: Paloma Villalobos has built a career on other people's voices, ghostwriting the memoirs of her former friend turned literary rival, Inés Duarte. When a letter she wrote eleven years ago—never sent, postmarked from the vineyard town where she once loved and fled—surfaces in a box of Inés's papers, Paloma must return to Valdemora to trace how it got there. There she finds Tomás Ferreira, the man the letter was meant for, now running his family's struggling vineyard and unaware of who she really is. As harvest approaches and Inés's memoir threatens to expose everything, Paloma must choose between remaining invisible and claiming her name, her past, and a love that refuses to stay in the past tense; she ends the book signing her own work for the first time, staying through the harvest with Tomás.
about_author: Rosalind Almeida is the pen name of a former translator who spent a decade rendering other writers' love stories into English before daring to write her own. She lives between Lisbon and a small coastal town whose train station closes at nine each night.

chapters.title: The Ghost's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In her Lisbon apartment, Paloma finishes a chapter of Inés Duarte's memoirs, erasing herself so thoroughly that even her punctuation disappears. Her agent calls with good news she can't share. The beat: competence as camouflage, and the quiet ache of uncredited work.

chapters.title: Postmark: Valdemora
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Sorting papers for Inés's archive, Paloma opens a box and finds her own handwriting—a letter written eleven years ago, never sent, postmarked Valdemora. Her hands shake. The beat: the past arriving with bureaucratic precision, demanding acknowledgment.

chapters.title: What Inés Knows
chapters.summary: Inés's POV. Inés watches Paloma react to the letter and says nothing, filing the moment away. She suspects the ghostwriter has a history she's been hiding. The beat: quiet menace of a rival who collects secrets like first editions.

chapters.title: The Last Train Rule
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Flashback to eleven years ago: young Paloma in Valdemora, falling for Tomás Ferreira among the vines, and the rule they made—that whoever stayed after the last train left was choosing to stay for good. She left on it. The beat: tender, doomed intimacy.

chapters.title: A Reasonable Excuse
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma invents research reasons to travel to Valdemora, telling herself it's about the letter's provenance, not the man. On the bus out of the city she rehearses apologies she'll never deliver. The beat: self-deception dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Man at the Gate
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Arriving at Quinta Ferreira, Paloma is recognized instantly by Tomás—who doesn't know she wrote the memoirs or why she vanished. His welcome is polite and glacial. The beat: the shock of being seen by someone she wronged.

chapters.title: Eleven Vintages
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Tomás reflects on eleven harvests without her, the vineyard his father nearly lost, and the letter he never received—or did he? A half-memory of an envelope surfaces. The beat: grief worn down into routine, with a crack of new suspicion.

chapters.title: Cellar Truths
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Working in the cellar to earn her keep, Paloma learns the vineyard is failing and that Tomás's sister Marta resents any stranger near the books. She finds a 2013 ledger page torn out. The beat: mystery deepening alongside physical closeness.

chapters.title: Marta's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta reveals she intercepted mail during their father's illness—including one letter she burned unread, believing it would break Tomás's heart again. Guilt has kept her silent for years. The beat: confession as both wound and relief.

chapters.title: Inés Calls Collect
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Inés phones with a deadline and a veiled threat: she knows where Paloma is, and the memoir's final chapter will 'tell the whole story' unless Paloma delivers something extraordinary. The beat: the cage of the ghostwriter's contract tightening.

chapters.title: Rain on the Trellis
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. A storm traps Paloma and Tomás in the winery overnight; the last train passes unheard through the rain. They talk until dawn—not forgiving, but finally accurate about what happened. The beat: honesty as the first form of intimacy.

chapters.title: The Draft Nobody Wrote
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma begins writing—in her own voice—for the first time in years: pages addressed to Tomás that are not the letter, but its living sequel. She hides them in her suitcase. The beat: identity stirring under long disuse.

chapters.title: First Fruit
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Harvest begins early; the whole valley mobilizes. Tomás catches himself planning around Paloma's presence and panics quietly. Marta warns him not to let her leave without answers this time. The beat: hope arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: The Rival Descends
chapters.summary: Inés's POV. Inés arrives in Valdemora unannounced, ostensibly to research terroir for the memoir, actually to confront the past she shares with both Paloma and—revealed here—the Ferreira family. The beat: the triangle becomes a square, and every side is armed.

chapters.title: Three at the Table
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A harvest dinner where Inés performs charm while dropping hints about 'a famous ghostwriter' in her book. Tomás goes still. Paloma realizes exposure is hours away. The beat: dread served with dessert.

chapters.title: Named in Print
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Tomás reads the leaked advance excerpt online: Paloma Villalobos, ghostwriter, and the story of a girl who left on the last train. He understands everything at once—the letter, the lies, the visit. The beat: betrayal reprocessed with full information.

chapters.title: The Empty Platform
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma waits at the closed station, ready to leave before sunrise, and finds Tomás there instead of a train. He asks only one question: why she never told him she'd written back. The beat: confrontation stripped of performance.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma recites the unsent letter from memory—eleven years of fear compressed into the truth: she left because staying meant becoming someone visible, and visibility had already cost her family everything. The beat: catharsis; the price of survival named aloud.

chapters.title: Inés's Last Chapter
chapters.summary: Inés's POV. Confronted privately, Inés admits her memoir's exposé was leverage born of envy—and of an old debt to the Ferreiras she'd rather bury than print. She offers Paloma a choice: co-credit or silence. The beat: rival softened into reluctant mirror.

chapters.title: Byline
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma sends her agent the finished manuscript with her own name on the cover and Inés's grudging agreement. Then she walks to the vineyard as the first grapes come in. The beat: claiming authorship of her own life.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. The last train leaves the station empty. Tomás waits at the gate anyway, and Paloma stays past it—deliberately, visibly, choosing. They walk the rows together in the dark. The beat: the old rule fulfilled in reverse.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, closing. Weeks later, the wine is pressed and the book is proofed; Paloma signs the dedication page in her own hand. Marta burns nothing more; Inés sends a single word: 'Finally.' The beat: inheritance reclaimed—of name, of land's rhythm, of love kept in the present tense.
